specStatements.text: The transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.
Students should be able to describe the difference compared with Group 1 in melting points, densities, strength, hardness and reactivity with oxygen, water and halogens.
Students should be able to exemplify these general properties by reference to Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
Many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts.
Students should be able to exemplify these general properties by reference to compounds of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.

scopeNotes.statement: exemplify these general properties by reference to Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every transition element used to illustrate melting point, density, strength, hardness or reactivity in this content is drawn from the six the specification names: chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper. No other transition element is required, and comparisons are made only against Group 1 metals, which is the comparison the specification asks for.

scopeNotes.statement: exemplify these general properties by reference to compounds of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Ion charges, compound colours and catalytic uses are illustrated only with compounds of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper. The specification asks for these properties to be exemplified, not explained, so no explanation of why d-block ions are coloured or catalytically active is given, and no electronic structure of transition elements is taught.

concepts.definition: The metals found in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. They are metals with similar properties to one another, and those properties are different from the properties of the elements in Group 1.

The metals in the first column of the periodic table, such as lithium, sodium and potassium. They are soft, have low melting points and low densities, and react vigorously with oxygen, water and the halogens.
Chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn), iron (Fe), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni) and copper (Cu). These are the transition elements the specification uses to exemplify the general properties of the block.

Transition elements have much higher melting points than Group 1 metals. Iron melts at about 1538 degrees C, copper at about 1085 degrees C and chromium at about 1907 degrees C, while sodium melts at about 98 degrees C and potassium at about 63 degrees C.

Transition elements are much denser than Group 1 metals. Iron has a density of about 7.9 g/cm3 and copper about 8.9 g/cm3, while lithium (0.53 g/cm3), sodium (0.97 g/cm3) and potassium (0.86 g/cm3) are less dense than water and float on it.

concepts.term: Strength and hardness compared with Group 1
concepts.definition: Transition elements are hard and strong, which is why iron, chromium and nickel are used in structures and tools. Group 1 metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife and are far too weak to be used structurally.

concepts.term: Reaction with oxygen compared with Group 1
concepts.definition: Group 1 metals react quickly with oxygen: a freshly cut surface tarnishes within seconds. Transition elements react with oxygen far more slowly. Iron rusts slowly in damp air, copper dulls slowly, and chromium and nickel form a thin protective oxide layer that keeps their surface shiny.

concepts.term: Reaction with water compared with Group 1
concepts.definition: Group 1 metals react vigorously with cold water, fizzing as hydrogen is released and forming an alkaline hydroxide solution, for example 2Na + 2H2O gives 2NaOH + H2. Transition elements such as chromium, nickel and copper react very slowly or not at all with cold water.

concepts.term: Reaction with halogens compared with Group 1
concepts.definition: Group 1 metals react vigorously with the halogens at once, for example 2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl. Transition elements react with halogens far less readily and usually need to be heated first, for example heated iron reacts with chlorine as 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.

Many transition elements form more than one kind of ion, each with a different charge. Iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+, copper forms Cu+ and Cu2+, chromium forms Cr2+ and Cr3+, and cobalt forms Co2+ and Co3+. Every Group 1 metal, by contrast, forms only a 1+ ion.

concepts.term: Roman numeral in a compound name
concepts.definition: Because a transition metal can form ions of different charges, its name carries a Roman numeral giving the charge on the metal ion. Iron(II) chloride is FeCl2, containing Fe2+; iron(III) chloride is FeCl3, containing Fe3+. The numeral is the charge, not a count of atoms.

Transition elements form coloured compounds, and the colour depends on the metal ion present. Copper(II) compounds are blue, iron(II) compounds are pale green, iron(III) compounds are orange-brown, nickel(II) compounds are green and potassium manganate(VII) is purple.

Compounds of the Group 1 metals are white solids that dissolve in water to give colourless solutions, such as sodium chloride and potassium bromide. A coloured compound or a coloured solution is therefore a sign that a transition metal is present.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up in the reaction. It is not a reactant, and it does not change the amount of product that can be made.

Transition elements and their compounds are useful as catalysts. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process that makes ammonia, nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of vegetable oils, and manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, 2H2O2 giving 2H2O + O2.

misconceptions.question: Does a piece of nickel fizz in cold water in the same way that potassium does?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium reacts vigorously with cold water and fizzes as hydrogen is given off. Nickel shows no visible reaction with cold water.
misconceptions.misconception: All metals react with water and fizz; transition metals just do it a bit more slowly than Group 1 metals do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactivity series is usually met as a single ranked list, which makes reactivity look like a difference of speed rather than a difference of whether a reaction happens at all. Rusting also gets described as iron reacting with water, so students conclude that iron and water react on contact.
misconceptions.correction: Group 1 metals react with cold water on contact. Transition elements such as chromium, nickel and copper react extremely slowly or not at all, which is exactly why copper is used for water pipes. Rusting is slow and needs both water and oxygen together over days or weeks, not seconds.

misconceptions.question: Iron is much harder and denser than sodium. Does that make iron the more reactive metal?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is harder, stronger and denser than sodium, and it is also far less reactive than sodium.
misconceptions.misconception: Transition metals are tough, heavy metals, so they must be the more powerful and more reactive ones; sodium is soft and light, so it must be weak in every sense.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word strong is used both for how hard a material is and for how vigorously a chemical reacts, so students carry one meaning into the other and expect physical toughness and chemical reactivity to go together.
misconceptions.correction: Physical properties and chemical reactivity are separate. Transition elements are hard, strong and dense and are much less reactive than Group 1 metals, which are soft, light and extremely reactive. Sodium is stored under oil for this reason, while iron girders sit outdoors for years.

misconceptions.question: Do all metals need a very high temperature before they melt?
misconceptions.correct: Transition elements have high melting points, but Group 1 metals melt at low temperatures: sodium melts at about 98 degrees C and potassium at about 63 degrees C.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals all melt at around a thousand degrees or more, because that is what metals are like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The metals students handle in everyday life are structural transition metals such as iron and copper, and furnaces and foundries reinforce the image of metal as something that needs enormous heat to melt.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the numbers directly. Iron melts at about 1538 degrees C and chromium at about 1907 degrees C, while potassium melts at about 63 degrees C, which is below the temperature of hot water from a kettle. Low melting point is one of the properties that separates Group 1 from the transition elements.

misconceptions.question: Sodium floats when it is dropped onto water. Is it being held up by the gas it makes?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium floats because its density, 0.97 g/cm3, is lower than the density of water. The hydrogen produced is not what keeps it up.
misconceptions.misconception: Every metal is denser than water and must sink, so a floating metal has to be resting on the bubbles of gas it is producing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students only ever see dense transition metals such as iron and copper sink, so floating looks impossible for a metal and the visible fizzing offers a ready explanation for it.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium (0.53 g/cm3), sodium (0.97 g/cm3) and potassium (0.86 g/cm3) are all less dense than water, so they float on it before, during and regardless of any reaction. Iron (7.9 g/cm3) and copper (8.9 g/cm3) are several times denser than water and sink.

misconceptions.question: Iron forms Fe2+ ions and Fe3+ ions. Do the two kinds of iron have different numbers of protons?
misconceptions.correct: Both are iron and both have 26 protons. Fe2+ has lost two electrons and Fe3+ has lost three electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: If the charge is different, something in the nucleus must be different, so Fe3+ must have an extra proton compared with Fe2+.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge has just been taught as a balance between protons and electrons, and the proton is the particle students associate with positive charge, so changing the charge feels like changing the protons.
misconceptions.correction: Changing the number of protons would change the element itself. Ion charge is set by electrons only: an iron atom with 26 protons and 26 electrons becomes Fe2+ by losing two electrons and Fe3+ by losing three. Forming ions with more than one charge is a general property of the transition elements.

misconceptions.question: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue. Is the sulfate what makes it blue?
misconceptions.correct: The colour comes from the transition metal ion. Copper(II) compounds are blue whether the compound is the sulfate, the chloride or the nitrate.
misconceptions.misconception: The non-metal part of the compound carries the colour, so all sulfates are blue and all chlorides are the same colour as each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper(II) sulfate is the blue solid students see most often in the laboratory, so blue becomes attached to the whole name, and sulfate is the unfamiliar half that seems more likely to be responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Test the idea against other compounds. Sodium sulfate is a white solid giving a colourless solution, while copper(II) chloride and copper(II) nitrate are both blue in solution. It is the copper(II) ion that is blue, and it is the transition metal that makes a compound coloured.

misconceptions.question: The iron catalyst in the Haber process has to be replaced each time. True or false?
misconceptions.correct: False. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so the same iron continues to work reaction after reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst is one of the ingredients, so it gets consumed like the other reactants and has to be topped up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Catalysts are written into the description of a reaction alongside the reactants and are clearly involved in it, so students treat them as another starting material being converted into product.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst is not a reactant and does not appear in the balanced equation. The iron in the Haber process provides a surface on which the reaction happens faster; it is chemically unchanged at the end and the same charge can be used for a long time.

misconceptions.question: Adding a catalyst gives you more product from the same amount of reactant. Is that right?
misconceptions.correct: No. A catalyst makes the reaction faster; it does not change how much product the reactants can make.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst improves the reaction, so it must increase the amount of product you end up with as well as the speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In an experiment that is stopped early, the catalysed reaction really has produced more so far, and students read that snapshot as a bigger final amount rather than as the same amount reached sooner.
misconceptions.correction: Let both reactions run to completion and the masses of product are the same; the catalysed one simply gets there first. The usefulness of transition metal catalysts is that they deliver the product faster and at lower cost, not that they create extra product.

misconceptions.question: Copper does not react with cold water. Does that mean it never reacts with oxygen either?
misconceptions.correct: Copper does react with oxygen, but slowly: its shiny surface dulls over time, and heated in air it forms black copper(II) oxide, 2Cu + O2 gives 2CuO.
misconceptions.misconception: Transition metals are unreactive metals, so they simply do not react with oxygen at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word unreactive is used as an absolute, and copper and chromium keep their appearance for so long that no reaction seems to be happening. Metals that form a protective oxide layer look permanently unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Less reactive does not mean unreactive. Transition elements react with oxygen far more slowly than Group 1 metals: iron rusts over weeks in damp air, copper dulls slowly, and chromium and nickel hold a thin oxide layer that protects the metal underneath.

misconceptions.question: Are all metal compounds white powders that dissolve to give colourless solutions?
misconceptions.correct: Group 1 compounds are white and give colourless solutions, but transition metal compounds are coloured, such as blue copper(II) sulfate and green nickel(II) chloride.
misconceptions.misconception: Compounds are white crystals like salt, and a solution of any of them will be clear and colourless.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first compounds students meet are sodium chloride and other Group 1 salts, and the word clear is often used loosely to mean colourless, which merges the two ideas.
misconceptions.correction: Colour is a diagnostic difference between the two sets of metals. Sodium chloride and potassium bromide are white and dissolve to colourless solutions; copper(II) sulfate is blue, iron(II) sulfate is pale green, and potassium manganate(VII) is purple. A coloured solution points to a transition metal.

misconceptions.question: In the name iron(III) chloride, does the III tell you there are three chlorine atoms?
misconceptions.correct: The III gives the charge on the metal ion, Fe3+. Three chloride ions happen to be needed to balance that charge, giving FeCl3.
misconceptions.misconception: The Roman numeral is just a way of counting the atoms of the other element in the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In iron(III) chloride the numeral and the number of chlorines match, so the wrong rule gives the right formula and is never challenged until a compound such as iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3, appears.
misconceptions.correction: Read the numeral as the charge on the metal ion, then balance the charges. Fe3+ with O2- needs two Fe3+ and three O2- to balance, giving Fe2O3, not FeO3. The numeral is needed only because transition elements form ions with different charges.

misconceptions.question: Do all transition metals form 2+ ions?
misconceptions.correct: Many transition elements form ions with several different charges, such as Fe2+ and Fe3+, Cu+ and Cu2+, and Cr2+ and Cr3+.
misconceptions.misconception: A transition metal has one fixed charge, 2+, in the same way that a Group 1 metal always has 1+.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group charges have just been taught as fixed and predictable from the group number, and copper(II) and iron(II) compounds are the ones most often seen in the laboratory, so 2+ looks like the standard transition metal charge.
misconceptions.correction: Position in the central block does not fix a single charge. Forming ions with different charges is itself one of the properties that distinguishes transition elements from Group 1, which is why their compounds need a Roman numeral in the name.

misconceptions.question: Would a knife blade cut through a lump of potassium?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Group 1 metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife, whereas transition elements such as chromium and iron are hard and strong.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals are hard by definition, so no metal could be sliced with an ordinary knife.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hardness is treated as part of what the word metal means, learnt from everyday metal objects that are all transition metals or their alloys, so a soft metal sounds like a contradiction.
misconceptions.correction: Hardness varies enormously between metals. Sodium and potassium can be cut with a knife and reveal a shiny surface that tarnishes within seconds; chromium and iron are hard and strong, which is why they are used for tools and structures.

misconceptions.question: When iron reacts with chlorine, can the chlorine be written as Cl in the equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chlorine gas exists as Cl2 molecules, so the balanced equation is 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.
misconceptions.misconception: The compound has single Cl atoms in its formula, so chlorine can be written as Cl on the left and the numbers made to fit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is practised as arithmetic on numbers of atoms, and writing Cl or O instead of Cl2 or O2 makes that arithmetic easier. The fact that some elements exist as molecules is learnt separately and is not brought to mind while balancing.
misconceptions.correction: Fix every formula first, then balance only by changing the large numbers in front. Chlorine gas is Cl2 and oxygen gas is O2, so the reactions the specification compares are written 2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl, 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3 and 2Cu + O2 gives 2CuO.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the transition elements compared with the elements in Group 1?

options.text: Metals that react with cold water even more vigorously than the Group 1 metals do
options.rationale: Students who treat reactivity as one continuous scale, and who know transition metals are the tougher ones, expect them to react harder with everything.

options.text: Metals with properties similar to each other but different from Group 1 metals
options.rationale: The specification states that the transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.

options.text: Metals that share no common properties at all, each one behaving in its own way
options.rationale: Seeing that iron forms two different ions suggests unpredictability, so students conclude the block has no shared pattern of behaviour.

options.text: Metals with exactly the same properties as Group 1 but with higher proton numbers
options.rationale: Students who know both sets are metals assume that being a metal fixes the properties and that position only changes the atomic number.

mcqs.stem: Iron melts at 1538 degrees C. Which value is the most likely melting point of sodium?

options.text: 1495 degrees C
options.rationale: A value close to iron's is chosen by students who believe every metal needs roughly the same very high temperature to melt.

options.text: 660 degrees C
options.rationale: This is aluminium's melting point, recalled from another context and offered as a middling metal value.

options.text: 98 degrees C
options.rationale: Group 1 metals have low melting points; sodium melts at about 98 degrees C, far below any transition element.

options.text: 3550 degrees C
options.rationale: Students who link vigorous reactivity with strong bonding expect the reactive Group 1 metal to be the hardest of all to melt.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of sodium floats on water, but a small piece of copper sinks. Why?

options.text: Sodium has a lower density than water, while copper is far denser than water
options.rationale: Sodium's density is 0.97 g/cm3, below water's 1.00 g/cm3, so it floats; copper's is 8.9 g/cm3, so it sinks. Low density is a Group 1 property.

options.text: Sodium is held up only by the bubbles of hydrogen gas that its reaction makes
options.rationale: The fizzing is the most obvious thing happening, so students who assume all metals are dense use the gas to explain the floating.

options.text: Sodium is much the softer of the two metals, and soft metals float on water
options.rationale: Softness and low density really do go together in Group 1, so students promote the coincidence into a cause.

options.text: Sodium reacts with the water, and a metal that is reacting stays at the surface
options.rationale: Reaction and floating are seen together every time sodium is demonstrated, so one looks like the reason for the other.

mcqs.stem: Which observation is evidence of the difference in hardness between Group 1 and the transition elements?

options.text: Sodium melts in a Bunsen flame, but iron only glows red and stays solid
options.rationale: This is a real difference between the two metals, but it is evidence about melting point rather than about hardness.

options.text: Sodium can be cut with a knife, but iron cannot be cut in that way at all
options.rationale: Resistance to being cut is exactly what hardness measures. Group 1 metals are soft enough to cut; transition elements are hard.

options.text: Sodium is kept under oil, but iron can be left standing in the open air
options.rationale: Students who merge toughness with reactivity read a storage difference as a strength difference; it is really about reactivity.

options.text: Sodium floats when placed on water, but iron sinks straight to the bottom
options.rationale: Floating is a density difference, but soft and light feel like the same idea, so this is picked as a hardness test.

mcqs.stem: Potassium and nickel are each added to separate beakers of cold water. What is seen?

options.text: Both metals fizz strongly, because every metal reacts with cold water somehow
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the reactivity series as a difference of speed rather than of whether any reaction occurs.

options.text: Nickel reacts faster, because it is the denser and the harder of the two metals
options.rationale: Physical toughness is read as chemical power, so the structural metal is expected to win any comparison.

options.text: Potassium fizzes vigorously, while nickel shows no visible reaction at all
options.rationale: Group 1 metals react vigorously with cold water, releasing hydrogen. Transition elements such as nickel react very slowly or not at all.

options.text: Neither metal reacts, because both of them need steam before anything happens
options.rationale: Students who have met the metal and steam reaction generalise it and forget that Group 1 metals react with cold water.

mcqs.stem: Heated iron wool reacts with chlorine gas to form iron(III) chloride. Which equation is correct?

options.text: 2Fe + 3Cl gives 2FeCl3
options.rationale: The atoms balance neatly this way, so students who treat balancing as arithmetic write chlorine as single atoms.

options.text: Fe + Cl2 gives FeCl2
options.rationale: A student who believes a transition metal is always 2+ writes iron(II) chloride, not the iron(III) chloride the question states.

options.text: 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3
options.rationale: Balanced, with 2 Fe and 6 Cl on each side, and chlorine correctly written as the diatomic molecule Cl2.

options.text: Fe + Cl3 gives FeCl3
options.rationale: The 3 in the product is copied back onto the element, treating the numeral as a count that must show on both sides.

mcqs.stem: Freshly cut sodium and freshly polished copper are both left out in air. What happens?

options.text: Sodium tarnishes in seconds, while copper's surface dulls only very slowly
options.rationale: Group 1 metals react rapidly with oxygen; transition elements react with oxygen much more slowly, as the specification requires students to describe.

options.text: Sodium tarnishes in seconds, while copper stays bright because it never oxidises
options.rationale: Copper keeps its shine for so long that students take less reactive to mean no reaction with oxygen at all.

options.text: Copper tarnishes first, because it is the denser and harder metal of the pair
options.rationale: Toughness is again read as chemical reactivity, so the structural metal is expected to react first.

options.text: Both tarnish at the same rate, since the air in the room affects metals equally
options.rationale: Students who see corrosion as something air does to metal expect the rate to depend on the air, not on the metal.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of ions illustrates a property typical of the transition elements?

options.text: Fe2+ and Ni2+, because every transition element forms an ion with a 2+ charge
options.rationale: The 2+ ions met most often in the laboratory make 2+ look like the fixed charge for the whole block.

options.text: Na+ and K+, because these are the ions formed by the most reactive of metals
options.rationale: Reactive is confused with typical of transition metals, and these are the two metal ions students recall most easily.

options.text: Fe3+ and Al3+, because an ion carrying a 3+ charge is unique to this block
options.rationale: Fe3+ is genuinely a transition metal ion, so the pairing looks right until aluminium's position in Group 3 is checked.

options.text: Fe2+ and Fe3+, because many transition elements form ions of different charges
options.rationale: One element forming ions of two different charges is the property the specification names, exemplified here by iron.

mcqs.stem: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl2 and FeCl3. What does the II in the name iron(II) chloride tell you?

options.text: There are two chlorine atoms in the formula of the compound
options.rationale: In this compound the numeral and the number of chlorines match, so the wrong rule appears to work perfectly.

options.text: The iron ion in the compound carries a charge of 2+
options.rationale: The Roman numeral states the charge on the metal ion, which is needed because transition elements form ions of different charges.

options.text: The iron atom holds two protons more than a normal one
options.rationale: Positive charge is associated with protons, so a change in charge is assumed to be a change in the nucleus.

options.text: Two iron ions are joined to each chloride ion present
options.rationale: The numeral is read as a count, and putting the two on the iron rather than the chlorine gives this variant of the same error.

mcqs.stem: Four white or coloured solids are each dissolved in water. Which one gives a coloured solution?

options.text: potassium sulfate
options.rationale: Students who think the sulfate carries the blue colour of copper(II) sulfate expect any sulfate to give a coloured solution.

options.text: potassium bromide
options.rationale: Bromine is a strongly coloured element, so its compounds are wrongly assumed to be coloured as well.

options.text: lithium carbonate
options.rationale: Picked by students who have not linked colour to the metal ion and so treat all four of these names as equivalent.

options.text: copper(II) sulfate
options.rationale: Copper is a transition element and its compounds are coloured: copper(II) sulfate gives a blue solution. The other three are Group 1 compounds.

mcqs.stem: What colour is a solution of potassium manganate(VII)?

options.text: colourless
options.rationale: The name begins with potassium, a Group 1 metal, so students expect the white solid and colourless solution of a Group 1 salt.

options.text: orange
options.rationale: Confused with potassium dichromate(VI), another laboratory oxidising agent whose solution really is orange.

options.text: purple
options.rationale: Manganese is a transition element and potassium manganate(VII) solution is a strong purple, a standard example of a coloured compound.

options.text: pale green
options.rationale: Pale green is recalled as a transition metal colour without checking which metal ion it belongs to; it is iron(II).

mcqs.stem: Iron is used in the Haber process to make ammonia. What is the iron doing?

options.text: It speeds up the reaction without itself being used up
options.rationale: This is what a catalyst does, and being useful as catalysts is the property the specification gives for transition elements.

options.text: It is used up steadily while the reaction it speeds up goes on
options.rationale: Catalysts are listed alongside the reactants, so students assume they are consumed in the same way.

options.text: It raises the greatest amount of ammonia that can be produced
options.rationale: A catalysed reaction has made more product at any early moment, which is misread as a larger final yield.

options.text: It reacts with the nitrogen to build the ammonia product
options.rationale: The iron is clearly essential to the process, so students place it among the reactants.

mcqs.stem: Which substance is used as the catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide?

options.text: sodium hydroxide
options.rationale: A very familiar laboratory bottle, chosen by students who have not connected catalysis with the transition elements.

options.text: manganese(IV) oxide
options.rationale: Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses 2H2O2 giving 2H2O + O2, exemplifying the catalytic property with a manganese compound.

options.text: iron(III) chloride
options.rationale: Students recall iron as the Haber process catalyst and assume any iron compound will catalyse any reaction.

options.text: copper(II) sulfate
options.rationale: The best known transition metal compound in the laboratory, offered because it is a transition metal compound at all.

mcqs.stem: Element X melts at 1495 degrees C, has a density of 8.9 g/cm3 and does not react with cold water. Which is X?

options.text: Potassium, because Group 1 metals are the strongest and densest metals
options.rationale: Students who link vigorous reactivity with physical toughness expect Group 1 to top every physical property.

options.text: Lithium, because it will not react with cold water at room temperature
options.rationale: Lithium is the least vigorous Group 1 metal with water, so its steady fizzing is remembered as no reaction.

options.text: Sodium, because every metal has a high melting point and high density
options.rationale: If all metals are assumed to melt high and be dense, the data cannot rule out a Group 1 metal.

options.text: Cobalt, because a transition element has a high melting point and density
options.rationale: All three pieces of data are transition element properties, and cobalt is one of the six named elements. Cobalt melts at 1495 degrees C.

mcqs.stem: Which set contains only transition elements?

options.text: Ni, Co, Na
options.rationale: Sodium is a metal that behaves dramatically, so students who define transition metals loosely as reactive metals include it.

options.text: Cr, Mn, Fe
options.rationale: Chromium, manganese and iron are all in the central block and are three of the six elements the specification names.

options.text: Fe, Cu, Ca
options.rationale: Calcium is a common metal met often in lessons, and its Group 2 position is not checked against the central block.

options.text: Cu, K, Cr
options.rationale: Potassium is included because two of the three are clearly transition metals and the set is judged as a whole.

mcqs.stem: Sodium and copper are each heated separately in chlorine gas. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Copper reacts far more vigorously, because it is the harder of the metals
options.rationale: Hardness is again taken as a measure of chemical vigour, so the tougher metal is expected to react harder.

options.text: Neither reacts, because chlorine only reacts with non-metal elements
options.rationale: Chlorine's reactions with non-metals are met first, so its vigorous reactions with metals are overlooked.

options.text: Both react equally fast, since chlorine attacks all metals in the same way
options.rationale: If the halogen is treated as the active partner, the identity of the metal seems not to matter.

options.text: Sodium reacts far more vigorously with the chlorine than copper does
options.rationale: Group 1 metals react vigorously with halogens; transition elements react far less readily and need heating, as with 2Fe + 3Cl2 giving 2FeCl3.

mcqs.stem: Iron forms both FeO and Fe2O3, but sodium forms only Na2O. Why is this?

options.text: Iron atoms can gain or lose protons, but sodium atoms are not able to
options.rationale: Charge is tied to protons in the student's mind, so two different charges suggest two different nuclei.

options.text: Iron is the heavier atom, so it can bond to more oxygen atoms than sodium
options.rationale: Mass is treated as bonding capacity, which fits the larger formula of Fe2O3 and so looks convincing.

options.text: Iron forms ions of more than one charge; sodium forms only the Na+ ion
options.rationale: FeO contains Fe2+ and Fe2O3 contains Fe3+. Forming ions with different charges is a property of transition elements; Group 1 metals form 1+ ions only.

options.text: Iron acts as a catalyst, so its compounds can take a number of forms
options.rationale: Two true statements about iron are joined by a false causal link, since catalysis is a separate property.

mcqs.stem: Copper is heated strongly in air and turns black. Which equation represents this reaction?

options.text: 2Cu + O2 gives 2CuO
options.rationale: Balanced, with 2 Cu and 2 O on each side and oxygen written as O2. The black solid formed is copper(II) oxide.

options.text: 2Cu + 2O gives 2CuO
options.rationale: Writing oxygen as separate atoms makes the numbers balance easily, but oxygen in the air exists as O2 molecules.

options.text: Cu + O2 gives CuO2
options.rationale: The formula is built by sharing out the atoms available rather than from the charges on the ions in the compound.

options.text: Cu + O2 gives 2CuO
options.rationale: Oxygen is balanced by placing a 2 in front of the product, and the copper is then left unbalanced.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a transition element being used as a catalyst?

options.text: nickel, in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils
options.rationale: Nickel speeds the addition of hydrogen to unsaturated oils and is not used up, exemplifying the catalytic property with nickel.

options.text: sodium, in its reaction with water to give hydrogen
options.rationale: The sodium is producing a gas quickly, which looks like speeding a reaction up, but it is a reactant and is used up.

options.text: copper, in the wiring that carries current in a plug
options.rationale: A genuine and familiar use of a transition metal, chosen by students who match the metal rather than the job it does.

options.text: iron, in the girders holding up a railway bridge
options.rationale: Iron is remembered as the Haber process catalyst, so any prominent use of iron is read as the catalytic one.

mcqs.stem: Which formula is iron(III) oxide?

options.text: FeO3
options.rationale: The Roman numeral is read as the number of oxygen atoms, the rule that works by luck for iron(III) chloride.

options.text: Fe3O
options.rationale: The same counting error, with the three attached to the metal that the numeral follows in the name.

options.text: FeO
options.rationale: Assuming iron is always 2+ gives the formula of iron(II) oxide instead of iron(III) oxide.

options.text: Fe2O3
options.rationale: Fe3+ and O2- balance as two Fe3+ to three O2-, giving Fe2O3, the orange-brown oxide of iron(III).
